sections.h: Luke 6–8: Luke's sermon, Luke's women, Luke's Mark
sections.b: Chapters 6–8 show Luke's methods side by side. He follows Mark for the Sabbath disputes, the Twelve and the block of parables and miracles (Luke 6:1–19; 8:4–56; Mark 2:23–3:19; 4:1–5:43), but trims Mark's Greek, drops Aramaic words, softens the disciples' failures and calls the lake a lake. Between them he sets the double-tradition Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49), shorter and sharper about money than Matthew's, and his own material: the widow's son at Nain, the woman who anointed Jesus' feet, and the women who supported the mission (Luke 7:11–17; 7:36–8:3). Themes that run through the whole book are all here: reversal of rich and poor, Jesus as a prophet like Elijah, meals with sinners, the faith of Gentiles, and women as disciples.

Luke's sermon is given on "a stretch of flat ground" after Jesus comes down from a night of prayer and the choosing of the Twelve (Luke 6:12–17). It is about thirty verses long against Matthew's 107, and it has four blessings matched by four woes on the rich, the full, the laughing and the praised. Love of enemies stands at its center, framed by "keep loving your enemies" (Luke 6:27, 35), with "Become compassionate, the way your Father is compassionate" (Luke 6:36) where Matthew has "perfect." It has nothing on the Law of Moses. Most scholars think both sermons go back to one collection of sayings, with Luke closer to its length and order; others think Luke abridged Matthew.

common: Luke's "Blessed are the poor" and Matthew's "poor in spirit" are usually seen as two forms of one saying.
uncommon: Some hold that Jesus preached the sermon on two occasions, once on a mountain and once on a plain.

sections.h: Blessed are the poor; woe to the rich (Luke 6:20–26)
sections.b: Luke's first beatitude names "the poor" without Matthew's "in spirit," and the next speak of hunger and tears "now." Four woes answer them: the rich have already been paid their comfort in full. The pattern continues Mary's song (Luke 1:52–53) and Jesus' Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:18), and anticipates the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31). Readers differ on how far the blessing concerns material poverty and how far the humble poor who trust God; the churches' answers are set out in a card at Luke 6:20.
sections.refs: Luke 6:20–26; Luke 1:52–53; Luke 4:18; Luke 7:22; Luke 16:19–31; Matthew 5:3

sections.b: In Luke 6:24 Jesus pronounces woe on the rich, who have their comfort "paid in full" now, a phrase taken from Greek receipts. In the explanation of the sower, Luke adds "pleasures" to Mark's worries and wealth as what chokes the word so that it never ripens (Luke 8:14). The same section shows wealth used well: women of means support Jesus' mission from their own property (Luke 8:3), and a centurion builds a synagogue (Luke 7:5).
sections.refs: Luke 6:24; Luke 8:14; Luke 8:3; Luke 7:5; Mark 4:18–19; 1 Enoch 94:8; James 5:1–6

sections.b: Jesus tells his followers to lend even to enemies "without hoping for anything back," going beyond the Law's command to lend freely to the poor (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–11). The Latin of this verse, mutuum date, nihil inde sperantes, became the main proof text for the medieval church's ban on all interest, until moral theologians and Reformers (Calvin above all) distinguished lending to the needy from commercial loans. The parable of the two debtors (Luke 7:41–43) uses canceled debt as a picture of forgiven sin. A card at Luke 6 sets out the churches' views.

Luke's version puts love of enemies first in the body of the sermon, right after the woes, and gives practical forms: do good to those who hate, bless those who curse, pray for abusers, offer the other cheek, let the robber take the tunic too, give and lend without return. Luke drops Matthew's "right" cheek and lawsuit, picturing a blow and a robbery instead (Luke 6:29; Matthew 5:39–40). The reason given is God's own kindness to the ungrateful and evil (Luke 6:35). Jesus and Stephen both pray for their killers (Luke 23:34; Acts 7:60).

Where Matthew has "be perfect," Luke has "Become compassionate (oiktirmones), the way your Father is compassionate" (Luke 6:36), using the Greek Old Testament's word for the LORD "compassionate and gracious" (Exodus 34:6). Luke then shows Jesus' own compassion: at Nain "the Lord's heart went out" to a widow who asked for nothing (Luke 7:13). The verse was the motto of the Catholic Jubilee of Mercy (2015–2016).

Luke tells the grain-field dispute and the healing of a withered right hand in quick succession. The disciples rub grain in their hands, which looked like threshing; Jesus answers with David and the Presence Bread and claims that the Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath, without Mark's saying that the Sabbath was made for human beings. In the synagogue he asks whether the day is for doing good or harm, saving life or destroying it, refusing the line between emergency healing (which Jewish law allowed) and healing that could wait. Codex Bezae adds at Luke 6:5 a saying about a man working on the Sabbath.

sections.h: The Twelve chosen after a night of prayer (Luke 6:12–16)
sections.b: Only Luke says Jesus spent the night praying before choosing the Twelve, and that he named them "apostles" (Luke 6:12–13). Luke's list differs from Mark's and Matthew's in having "Simon, who was called the Zealot" (a translation of Mark's "Cananaean") and "Judas son of James" in place of Thaddaeus. The same list, minus Judas Iscariot, appears in Acts 1:13. Luke sometimes names John before James (Luke 8:51; Luke 9:28; Acts 1:13), though more often "James and John" (Luke 5:10; Luke 6:14; Luke 9:54).

Hearing of Jesus' deeds, the imprisoned John sends two disciples to ask, "Are you the Coming One, or should we wait for someone else?" Jesus heals in front of them and answers with Isaiah's signs (Isaiah 35:5–6; 26:19; 61:1). He then praises John as more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1, and greater than anyone born of a woman, yet less than the least in God's kingdom. Luke adds that the tax collectors who had been baptized by John "declared that God was in the right," while the Pharisees and lawyers refused (Luke 7:29–30).
sections.refs: Luke 7:18–35; Matthew 11:2–19; Isaiah 35:5–6; Isaiah 61:1; Malachi 3:1; Luke 3:15–20; Luke 16:16

sections.b: Luke alone tells of a widow at Nain whose only son is being carried out to burial. Without her son she had lost her support. Jesus, moved with compassion, stops the bier and gives the young man back "to his mother," in the words of Elijah's miracle for the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:23). Luke has more widows than any other Gospel (Luke 2:37; 4:25–26; 18:1–8; 20:47; 21:1–4).

sections.h: Jesus as a prophet like Elijah (Luke 7)
sections.b: After citing Elijah's help for a widow of Sidon and Elisha's for a Syrian (Luke 4:25–27), Luke tells of Jesus healing a Gentile's servant and raising a widow's only son near Shunem, where Elisha raised a boy (2 Kings 4:8–37). He gives the son "to his mother" as Elijah did (1 Kings 17:23), and in Luke 8:55 the girl's spirit returns as the boy's life came back in 1 Kings 17:22. The crowd concludes: "A great prophet has been raised up among us!"

Luke tells two raisings in quick succession: a widow's son on his way to burial and Jairus' twelve-year-old daughter. Jesus speaks to the dead ("Young man, I tell you, get up"; "Child, get up") and calls death sleep. These are returns to ordinary life, signs of the resurrection to come. Jesus lists "the dead are raised" among the signs for John (Luke 7:22), and Peter raises Tabitha in the same pattern (Acts 9:36–42).

sections.h: The forgiven woman at the Pharisee's table (Luke 7:36–50)
sections.b: A woman known as a sinner anoints Jesus' feet at Simon the Pharisee's dinner. Jesus tells of two debtors whose debts were canceled and asks which will love more, then declares that her many sins have been forgiven, "for she has loved much," and that her faith has saved her. Whether her love was the cause or the evidence of forgiveness divides readers; a card at Luke 7 gives the churches' views. In the sermon, Jesus calls his followers to "release" others as they will be released (Luke 6:37).

Luke's anointing is set in Galilee at a Pharisee's house early in the ministry, not in Bethany before the Passover as in Mark 14:3–9, Matthew 26:6–13 and John 12:1–8. The woman wets Jesus' feet with tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them with perfumed oil. Jesus contrasts her with his host, who did not anoint his head with oil. Whether the Gospels tell of one event or two is debated.

Luke introduces Mary "known as Magdalene," from Magdala on the lake, as one of the women Jesus had freed from evil spirits: seven demons had gone out of her. She traveled with Jesus and helped pay for the mission (Luke 8:1–3), and she was among the women at the empty tomb (Luke 24:10). Luke places her directly after the unnamed sinful woman of Luke 7:36–50, which helped the later Western identification of the two, made by Gregory the Great in 591 and dropped from the Roman calendar in 1969. The Gospel itself does not link them.

common: Mary Magdalene was a repentant prostitute (a later Western tradition, not stated in any Gospel).

sections.h: Women who followed and supported Jesus (Luke 8:1–3)
sections.b: Only Luke names women traveling with Jesus in Galilee: Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Herod's steward Chuza, Susanna "and many others," who "served" the group from their own means (Luke 8:3). The verb diakoneō is the root of "deacon." Mary Magdalene and Joanna reappear as the first witnesses of the empty tomb (Luke 24:10). Scholars debate whether Luke presents women as disciples and patrons on a par with men, or praises them mainly in supporting roles.

Luke's sower follows Mark's but shortens it: the seed is trampled as well as eaten, falls on rock and withers for lack of moisture, and yields only a hundredfold. In the explanation, "the seed is the word of God," the devil takes it away "to keep them from believing and being saved," the rocky hearers fall away "in a season of testing," and the good soil bears fruit "by endurance." Luke keeps only a short echo of Isaiah 6:9–10 here and quotes it in full at the end of Acts. Chapter 7 adds two short parables: children in the market (Luke 7:31–35) and two debtors (Luke 7:41–43).

Luke sets the story in "the land of the Gerasenes, which is across from Galilee," Jesus' only visit to Gentile territory in this Gospel. The manuscripts name the place as Gerasenes, Gergesenes or Gadarenes. Luke adds that the demons begged not to be sent into the Abyss and that the man had been "saved," and he has Jesus send the man to tell his own town, not the Decapolis as in Mark 5:20, what God had done for him.

Several scenes touch on purity: Jesus lays his hand on a bier (Luke 7:14; compare Numbers 19:11–16), a sinful woman touches his feet (Luke 7:39), he meets a man living among tombs where pigs are kept (Luke 8:27, 32; compare Isaiah 65:4), a woman with a long flow of blood touches his tassel (Luke 8:43–44; Leviticus 15:25–27), and he takes a dead girl's hand (Luke 8:54). In each, instead of uncleanness passing to Jesus, life passes from him. Scholars caution that impurity under the Law was not sin and did not exclude a person from ordinary life.
sections.refs: Luke 7:14; Luke 8:27–33; Luke 8:43–48; Luke 8:54; Numbers 19:11–16; Leviticus 15:25–27; Isaiah 65:4

sections.h: The tassel touched by a sick woman (Luke 8:44)
sections.b: The woman with a flow of blood touches "the tassel of his cloak" (kraspedon), the tassel the Law required on every Israelite garment (Numbers 15:38). Luke, like Matthew 9:20, mentions the tassel; Mark 5:27 says only "his cloak." The detail shows Jesus dressed as an observant Jew.

A centurion in Capernaum, who loves the Jewish nation and built its synagogue, sends Jewish elders and then friends to Jesus, and says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. Jesus is amazed and says he has not met such faith even in Israel. The story anticipates Cornelius, another God-fearing centurion praised by Jews, in Acts 10. Luke's story also includes Gentiles from the coast of Tyre and Sidon among Jesus' hearers (Luke 6:17) and a Gentile man freed and sent home as a witness (Luke 8:26–39).

sections.h: The man working on the Sabbath (Codex Bezae at Luke 6:5)
sections.b: Codex Bezae (D, 400s) moves Luke 6:5 after 6:10 and puts in its place: "On the same day he saw a man working on the Sabbath and said to him, 'Man, if you know what you are doing, you are blessed. But if you do not know, you are cursed and a breaker of the Law.'" No other Gospel manuscript has it. Joachim Jeremias thought it might preserve a genuine saying; most scholars regard it as an early tradition inserted by a scribe. It is set out as a variant reading at Luke 6:5.

Jesus contrasts his host Simon, who gave him no water for his feet, no kiss of greeting and no oil for his head, with the woman who washed his feet with tears, kissed them and anointed them. Whether Simon's omissions were an insult (Kenneth Bailey) or simply ordinary (Amy-Jill Levine's caution) is debated. The scene is one of several meals in Luke at which Jesus is a guest of Pharisees (Luke 11:37; 14:1).

sections.h: Jesus' mother and brothers in Luke (Luke 8:19–21)
sections.b: Luke tells of Jesus' mother and brothers arriving and being unable to reach him for the crowd, but without Mark's earlier report that his family thought he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Jesus calls those who hear the word of God and do it his mother and brothers. The question of who the brothers were is discussed at Mark 6:3.

Luke 6–8 defines a disciple by hearing and doing: the builder who "listens to my words and acts on them" (Luke 6:47), the good soil that holds the word fast and bears fruit by endurance (Luke 8:15), and Jesus' true family, "the people who hear the word of God and do it" (Luke 8:21). The traveling company of Luke 8:1–3, the Twelve and the women, shows what following looks like on the road.
